results.title: Alien: Romulus facehuggers
results.brief_description:
Small, slippery and hard to stop, facehuggers are among cinema’s most dreaded creations. Since they first appeared in Ridley Scott’s Alien (1979), they’ve terrified space travellers and audiences alike. Once attached, escape is almost impossible.

Set between Alien and James Cameron’s Aliens (1986), Alien: Romulus (2024) brings the facehuggers back to deep space. Aboard the Romulus, they attack alone and in swarms. To create this range of action, Wētā Workshop broke the scenes down by movement, and carefully assessed what kind of actions the facehuggers needed to achieve across the movie. In total, the team made 73 facehuggers, all with different dynamic purposes. These included remote-controlled versions for scuttling across the floor, spring loaded attack versions, waterproof swimmers and tougher puppets that could be thrown across the set.

For some attacks, puppeteers used spring-loaded limbs, giving the facehugger’s long fingers and legs a gripping tension. The puppet was pulled off an actor, then the shot was played in reverse, making the creature appear to leap on and clamp down with terrifying force.

The hero facehugger was built for the most detailed shots in Alien: Romulus (2024). Wētā Workshop looked back to the facehuggers made by Stan Winston Studio for Aliens (1986), then developed a new puppet with greater precision and control.

The hero facehugger puppet used 30 servos – small motors that move specific parts – giving it 30 points of movement control. Depending on the shot, cables ran from the creature’s back or underneath its tail. One puppeteer could control the limb movements with a tablet and joysticks, while another guided the body with a rod. This gave the facehugger sharp, coordinated movement, making every curl, grip and reach feel deadly.
